rationale: A wins because it has discipline: "On says its subscription closes the loop on shoe waste. It hasn't said how much of the loop closes." is a real accountability angle with the missing proof named in plain English. B has useful bones, but it starts inflating beyond the brief with "does the rest of the running category have to follow?" and "moving a core product line to this model." That is how a real launch turns into speculative trade-mag fog.
gaps_in_A: "funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the investor/unit-economics angle; no funding event exists in the update.
"major athletic brand" is a small overreach. The update gives public, profitable, fast-growing; make the source prove major before pitching it.
"A profitable, fast-growing sneaker company" blurs the supplied fact. This is a running-shoe subscription, not a broad sneaker-company story unless On wants that framing.
It could have tested whether "castor-bean-based material" deserves a separate materials/manufacturing angle, but only if On has performance and sourcing data.
gaps_in_B: "moving a core product line to this model" is invented. The update says Cyclon subscription, not core product line.
"trading one-time sale revenue for smaller recurring payments" is too confident. The monthly price and lifetime economics are undisclosed, so "smaller" is a guess wearing a tie.
"does the rest of the running category have to follow?" is padded competitor drama. No competitor facts, analyst view, or category pressure is in the update.
"comparison to other circular-fashion claims later found overstated" imports a scandal frame the facts do not earn. Ask for recycling data first; don't staple borrowed suspicion onto it.
